summary: Investor residence in five Asian countries. The Philippines is best documented: the Philippine Retirement Authority's annual reports and the Commission on Audit give SRRV enrolments by year and nationality (about 3,600-7,800 a year, 60,022 active holders at end-2025, Chinese the largest group) and deposit rules back to 2006. Malaysia's MM2H has parliamentary replies with approvals by nationality to 2019, its 2021 and 2024 rule changes, and press-reported totals to 2024 (58,468 approvals). Thailand Privilege publishes only its latest year as open data (3,941 cards sold and 2,894 million baht in FY2025; 39,538 members). Indonesia's golden visa has two official counts (1,274 issued by May 2026). South Korea has official rule changes but only press-reported counts. Malaysia's Premium Visa Programme has no official source.

programs.name: Malaysia My Second Home (MM2H) / Program Malaysia Rumah Keduaku
programs.notes: Long-term social visit pass with multiple-entry visa for foreigners who show money in Malaysia; not permanent residence and no route to citizenship (minister, Feb 2026). Run by the Ministry of Tourism (MOTAC) with the Home Ministry and Immigration Department; Immigration (JIM) took over processing from August 2021 and MOTAC's One Stop Centre runs it again under the 2024 rules. No act of parliament: it is an administrative programme using passes under the Immigration Act and Immigration circulars (e.g. Pekeliling Imigresen Bil. 6/2009). Until 2020: 10-year pass, fixed deposit of about RM150,000-350,000 and offshore income of RM10,000 a month. New applications frozen in 2020; revived from October 2021 with RM1m deposit, RM40,000 monthly income, RM1.5m liquid assets and 5-year passes. Since June 2024: Platinum (US$1m deposit, RM2m home, 20 years), Gold (US$500k, RM1m home, 15 years), Silver (US$150k, RM600k home, 5 years) and a Special Economic/Financial Zone category (US$32k-65k, Forest City homes, 10 years). Sarawak runs its own S-MM2H (not covered here).

programs.name: Premium Visa Programme (PVIP)
programs.notes: Immigration Department scheme launched 1 Sept 2022 giving wealthy foreigners a 20-year residence pass for a RM200,000 participation fee (RM100,000 per dependant reportedly), a RM1m fixed deposit and RM40,000 monthly offshore income; applications through appointed agents only, quota of 20,000 in phase one. No official programme page or statistics were found on imi.gov.my in October 2026, so its current status is not confirmed.

programs.name: Thailand Privilege Card (Thailand Elite until 2023)
programs.notes: Paid membership sold by Thailand Privilege Card Co. (formerly Thailand Elite Card Co.), a state enterprise owned by the Tourism Authority of Thailand, that comes with a long-stay 'privilege entry' visa for the membership period plus concierge services. It is a fee, not an investment that can be recovered. Packages before October 2023 (Thailand Elite) are discontinued; since then Gold (900,000 baht, 5 years), Platinum (1.5m, 10 years), Diamond (2.5m, 15 years), Reserve (5m, 20 years) and Bronze (650,000 baht, 5 years). No route to permanent residence or citizenship. Launch year 2003 is from general knowledge of the scheme and not checked against a document here.

programs.name: Long-Term Resident (LTR) visa - Wealthy Global Citizens category
programs.notes: Ten-year renewable visa run by the Board of Investment, open since 1 September 2022, in four categories; only 'Wealthy Global Citizens' requires an investment: US$500,000 in Thai government bonds, Thai companies or Thai property, plus US$1m in assets and health insurance. Visa fee 50,000 baht per person. No route to permanent residence or citizenship is part of the scheme.

programs.name: Special Resident Retiree's Visa (SRRV)
programs.notes: Permanent non-immigrant visa with indefinite stay for foreign retirees (and former Filipinos) who place a visa deposit with a PRA-accredited bank, run by the Philippine Retirement Authority (PRA), a government corporation created by Executive Order 1037 (4 July 1985), placed under the Board of Investments in 2001 (EO 26) and attached to the Department of Tourism by the Tourism Act of 2009 (RA 9593). Options: SMILE (deposit kept in the bank), Classic (deposit can be converted into a condo purchase or long lease), Human Touch (ailing retirees), Courtesy (former Filipinos, retired diplomats). Deposits were cut in May 2006; since August 2025 the 'Expanded SRRV' sets minimum age 40 and deposits of US$15,000-50,000 depending on age and pension. The deposit is refunded when the retiree leaves the programme. No path to citizenship is part of the scheme.

programs.name: Special Investor's Resident Visa (SIRV)
programs.notes: Indefinite residence for foreigners aged 21+ who invest at least US$75,000 in a listed company, an Investment Priority Plan project, or manufacturing or services; issued by the Bureau of Immigration through the Board of Investments' One Stop SIRV Center. Legal basis usually given as Executive Order 226 (Omnibus Investments Code of 1987) and EO 63; not checked in the text of the orders here. No official counts found.

programs.name: Real-estate investment immigration (부동산 투자이민제), renamed tourism and resort facility investment immigration (관광·휴양시설 투자이민제) in 2023
programs.notes: Foreigners who buy tourism or resort property above a threshold in areas designated by the Minister of Justice (Jeju, Incheon Songdo/Yeongjong/Cheongna, Busan Haeundae/East Busan, Pyeongchang Alpensia, Yeosu Gyeongdo) get a residence (F-2) visa and, after keeping the investment five years, permanent residence (F-5). Legal basis: Immigration Act Enforcement Decree (F-2/F-5 status) and Ministry of Justice notices; in Jeju also the Jeju Special Act art. 147. Threshold in Jeju 500 million won from 2010, 1 billion won everywhere from 1 May 2023, when investment was limited to resort condominiums, lodging and tourist pensions in tourism zones. Permanent residence leads to local voting rights, which drove the 2023 tightening. Overwhelmingly used by Chinese nationals.

programs.name: Public-project investment immigration (공익사업 투자이민제)
programs.notes: Foreigners who place money in a public-interest fund run by the Korea Development Bank (principal returned without interest after five years, lent to small firms) or in designated development projects get F-2 residence and, after five years, F-5 permanent residence; the high-value scheme gives F-5 immediately on a pledge to keep the investment five years. General scheme 500m won (from May 2013), retirement scheme 300m won for 55+ (May 2013, abolished 29 June 2023), high-value 1.5bn won (Oct 2014). From 29 June 2023: 1.5bn and 3bn won.

programs.name: Golden Visa Indonesia
programs.notes: Five- or ten-year limited-stay permit (renewable) run by the Directorate General of Immigration, launched 25 July 2024, for corporate investors, individual investors (with or without founding a company), global talent, 'second home', 'silver hair' retirees, world figures, former Indonesians and descendants, and investors in the new capital (IKN). Individual investors who do not found a company place US$350,000 (5 years) or US$700,000 (10 years) in Indonesian government bonds, listed shares or deposits; those founding a company invest US$2.5m/US$5m; corporate directors US$25m/US$50m. No guarantor needed. The implementing regulation (a Minister of Law and Human Rights regulation on visas and stay permits, 2023-2024) could not be downloaded and is not cited. Separate from the Global Citizen of Indonesia (GCI) permit of January 2026 for diaspora.

new_indicators.name: Investor residence permits cancelled or terminated (all reasons)
new_indicators.definition: Programme residence visas or memberships ended in a period for any reason, mostly at the holder's request (e.g. a retiree leaving the Philippine SRRV and withdrawing the visa deposit), plus any cancelled by the authorities. Wider than residence_permits_revoked, which counts only withdrawals by the authorities.
new_indicators.notes: Used for the Philippine SRRV 'cancellations' series.

new_indicators.name: Residence-linked memberships sold
new_indicators.definition: Paid memberships sold in a period under a scheme that grants a long-stay visa as part of a membership package (e.g. Thailand Privilege / Thailand Elite cards), counted by card as the operator reports, including upgrades if the operator counts them (say so in notes).
new_indicators.notes: Not the same as visas issued: a family package may cover several people, and visas are issued separately by immigration.

new_indicators.name: Members of a residence-linked membership scheme (stock)
new_indicators.definition: Persons holding a valid membership on a date in a scheme that grants a long-stay visa as part of the membership (e.g. Thailand Privilege), all packages including discontinued ones unless noted.

gaps: Malaysia: no official annual series of MM2H approvals after 2019. Approvals for 2021-2025 and by tier exist only in press reports (e.g. 3,172 approvals in 2025, Silver 2,650, per IMI Daily citing the tourism minister on 25 Mar 2026); the IMI Daily page blocks downloads and we could not find the original statement, so these are not recorded.

Malaysia: the minister's written reply of 24 Feb 2025 (58,468 approvals) and oral reply of 4 Feb 2026 were not found on parlimen.gov.my; recorded from NST and Malay Mail. The full Auditor-General's 2019 Series 2 chapter on MM2H and the PAC's December 2021 report were not downloaded.

Malaysia: no official page, regulation or statistics for the Premium Visa Programme (PVIP) were found on imi.gov.my; its rules come from a Bernama report and a consultancy. Number of PVIP passes issued unknown.
Malaysia: the Home Ministry's 11 Aug 2021 MM2H statement (admin.moha.gov.my) timed out: download blocked.
Malaysia: Sarawak's separate S-MM2H programme was not researched.

Thailand: only the latest year (FY2568) of Thailand Privilege sales, revenue and members was found as data; earlier years (Thailand Elite since 2003, losses, the 2017 relaunch, member numbers by year) need the older annual reports. The FY2568 annual report (about 150 MB) stalled on download; the audited 2568 financial statements are image-only and were not read.

Thailand: prices of the pre-October 2023 Thailand Elite packages (Easy Access, Family Excursion, Superiority Extension, Ultimate Privilege) and the original 2003 card are not recorded: the official page lists none. Bronze launch date not found.
Thailand: no count of LTR visas issued (overall or Wealthy Global Citizen category) was found on ltr.boi.go.th.

Indonesia: the legal basis (Permenkumham on visas and stay permits, 2023, and its 2024 amendment for golden visas) could not be downloaded (peraturan.go.id unreachable, peraturan.bpk.go.id blocked by Cloudflare). No breakdown of golden visas by category count, only by investment value.

Philippines: PRA annual reports 2013-2015, 2018 and 2022-2024 were not read (2015, 2018, 2022-2024 are scanned or very large); so the gross enrolment and cancellation series has gaps 2020-2023 and cancellations after 2012. No official SIRV statistics; BOI pages (boi.gov.ph) return 403 and DFA consular pages are behind Cloudflare.

South Korea: no official annual statistics on investor-immigration F-2/F-5 grants were found; figures come from press reports of MOJ data given to MPs and from Jeju Province. The MOJ immigration statistics yearbook may have them (not checked). Thresholds outside Jeju before 2023 (e.g. Incheon, Busan, Pyeongchang) are not recorded. Whether the five areas were extended again in 2026 was not checked.
Web-search budget for the session ran out during the work, so Indonesian and Thai-language press searches were limited.
